# Introduction {#sec-intro}

According to Gallup, 22 percent of American workers worried technology would make their job obsolete in 2023, up seven percentage points from 2021 [@Gallup2023]. Concerns about automation were already evident years earlier. In 2017, the Pew Research Center reported that Americans expected automation to displace workers, although only 30 percent considered it likely that their own job would be replaced within their lifetime [@Pew2017]. These concerns reflect subjective expectations about future disruption rather than empirical evidence of current labor market conditions. Displacement reaches households through lost income, and what that income secures depends on local prices. Evaluating whether those concerns are reflected in local economic conditions requires an outcome that captures how households experience labor market disruption.

Median household income does not tell the full story of what residents can afford. Differences in local prices mean that the value of the same income can vary substantially across counties [@Moretti2013]. Purchasing power accounts for these differences by adjusting county median household income with Bureau of Economic Analysis Regional Price Parities. Measuring how that outcome relates to local work requires a way to describe the work itself.

Three studies established the framework we build on. @Autor2003 showed that computers substitute for routine tasks and complement non-routine ones, which makes it possible to identify occupations exposed to automation. Applying that idea to local labor markets, @AutorDorn2013 documented polarization in routine intensive areas, where employment grew at both the high and low ends of the wage distribution while middle wage employment declined. @AcemogluAutor2011 then generalized the argument into a model in which tasks are the unit of production and skill groups compete to supply them.

Nevertheless, none of this work speaks directly to purchasing power at the county level. These studies report outcomes in unadjusted wages and employment counts rather than in what those wages buy locally. They work at a broader labor market geography than the county. They also fit linear specifications, which leaves open whether purchasing power moves with task groups in fixed dollar steps or in proportion. These distinctions reflect differences in research purpose rather than flaws in the earlier work.

Across the counties analyzed here, which together hold about 84 percent of the United States population [@census_popest2023], routine work averaged 39 percent of task content in 2023. The middle half of counties ranged from 35 to 43 percent. This study examines whether a county's task groups are associated with purchasing power after accounting for poverty and unemployment, estimating associations rather than causal effects. We use a county by year panel from 2008 to 2023, excluding 2020, with 840 counties and 11,983 observations. County employment is classified into four task groups, shown in @fig-taskframework. @sec-data describes the data and construction of the panel.

```{python}
#| label: fig-taskframework
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "**The Four Task Groups.** Each occupation falls in one cell of the Autor (2003) task framework. Routine tasks follow explicit rules that a machine can be programmed to carry out; non-routine tasks require judgment, adaptability, or in person interaction. Cognitive tasks work primarily with information; manual tasks work with physical objects and people. Occupation groupings follow Autor and Dorn (2013). Non-routine cognitive, outlined with a dashed border, is the reference group omitted from the regression."
%%R -w 8.5 -h 6 -u in -r 150 -b transparent
quad_df <- data.frame(
  group = c("Non-Routine Cognitive", "Non-Routine Manual", "Routine Cognitive", "Routine Manual"),
  col = c(2, 2, 1, 1),
  row = c(2, 1, 2, 1),
  examples = c("Management, engineering,\nteaching", "Food service, care work,\ncleaning",
               "Clerical, sales,\nclaims processing", "Production, assembly,\nmachine operation"),
  is_reference = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)
)
quad_df$group_label <- gsub(" ", "\n", quad_df$group)
quad_df$linetype <- ifelse(quad_df$is_reference, "dashed", "solid")
quad_df$linewidth <- ifelse(quad_df$is_reference, 1.3, 0.9)

box_w <- 0.42; box_h <- 0.42

col_headers <- data.frame(
  col = c(1, 2),
  label = c("Routine", "Non-Routine")
)
row_headers <- data.frame(
  row = c(2, 1),
  label = c("Cognitive", "Manual")
)

ggplot(quad_df) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin=col-box_w, xmax=col+box_w, ymin=row-box_h, ymax=row+box_h,
                color=group, linetype=linetype, linewidth=linewidth),
            fill="#FCFCFB") +
  geom_text(aes(x=col, y=row+0.14, label=group_label, color=group),
            fontface="bold", size=4.6, lineheight=0.95) +
  geom_text(aes(x=col, y=row-0.20, label=examples), color="#52514E", size=3.1, lineheight=1.0) +
  geom_text(data=col_headers, aes(x=col, y=2.65, label=label),
            fontface="bold", size=4.3, color="#0B0B0B", inherit.aes=FALSE) +
  geom_text(data=row_headers, aes(x=0.52, y=row, label=label),
            hjust=1, size=3.6, color="#0B0B0B", lineheight=0.95, inherit.aes=FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("Non-Routine Cognitive"="#fc8d62", "Non-Routine Manual"="#e78ac3", "Routine Cognitive"="#66c2a5", "Routine Manual"="#8da0cb"), guide="none") +
  scale_linetype_identity() +
  scale_linewidth_identity() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0.05, 2.55), ylim=c(0.5, 2.85), clip="off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.margin=margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
        plot.background=element_rect(fill=NA, color=NA),
        plot.title=element_text(face="bold", size=13, hjust=0.5)) +
  labs(title="The Four Task Groups")
```

We estimate a panel regression with year indicators and standard errors clustered by county, which accounts for the dependence among repeated observations of the same county. Diagnostics on that specification motivated a log respecification. Random forest and neural network models then tested whether additional flexibility captured structure the linear specification missed. @sec-analysis describes the modeling strategy and diagnostics.

Our primary finding is that a one percentage point shift from non-routine cognitive work to non-routine manual work is associated with roughly \$846 less in purchasing power, with a 95 percent interval of plus or minus \$38, evaluated at the panel mean. Task groups can be measured for any county from public data, and they carry information about local economic conditions that poverty and unemployment rates alone do not. That makes them useful to policymakers and economic development agencies deciding where to direct resources.
